title: Phones, sleep and the evidence

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: The sleep study came out today. Students who keep the phone out of the bedroom got about forty minutes more sleep a night. Forty minutes.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Out of the bedroom entirely, or just not in the bed?

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Out of the room. Charging somewhere else.

turns.speaker: Oliver
turns.text: I'd want to know who agreed to do that, though. The kind of person who'll put their phone in the hallway for a month is probably already sleeping better than the rest of us.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Yeah, that's the thing that always gets me with these.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: You're not measuring the phone. You're measuring the sort of person who volunteers.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: They randomised it, actually. Same pool, half told to move it, half told to carry on.

turns.speaker: Oliver
turns.text: Oh. Well, that's a better study than I assumed.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: And the interesting bit is it wasn't the blue light. They tested that separately and the filters made almost no difference.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: So it's just that the thing is interesting.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Basically. It's not the screen, it's the fact that there's always one more thing on it.

turns.speaker: Oliver
turns.text: Which would explain why the night mode setting never did anything for me. I still lay there for an hour, only in orange.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Honestly, that's the most convincing part of the whole thing.

points: A study found students who charged their phones outside the bedroom slept about forty minutes more per night.
Oliver raises self-selection: people willing to move their phone may already sleep better.
Ben agrees the study might be measuring the type of volunteer rather than the phone.
Sofia answers that the study was randomised from one pool, which removes that objection.
The effect was not blue light: filters tested separately made almost no difference.
They conclude the cause is engagement rather than the screen itself, since there is always one more thing to look at, which is why night mode settings do not help.
